title: Futures slip as Nvidia gives back part of its record rally
dek: US stock futures are lower after Monday's best day for the S&P 500 and Nasdaq since April 2025, with Nvidia down 3% to 5% pre-market after its 31% jump. Treasury yields are slightly lower, a December Fed hike is still seen as near-certain, and Sanofi's $41 billion deal for Insmed leads company news.
quick: S&P 500 futures are down roughly 0.7% to 1% and Nasdaq 100 futures more, after Monday's 4.7% S&P gain and 6.5% Nasdaq surge.
Nvidia is down about 3% to 5% pre-market after soaring 31.5% to $165.05 on Jensen Huang's reinstatement as CEO.
Sanofi agreed to buy Insmed for $175 a share in cash, about $41 billion; Insmed is up about 14% and Sanofi more than 4% in Paris.
Asian chip stocks caught up with Wall Street: Taiwan's Taiex rose about 9% and South Korea's Kospi about 7%, back above 5,000.
The 10-year Treasury yield is near 4.90%, down about 2 basis points; futures still price roughly a 95% chance of a December Fed hike.
Today: consumer confidence at 10 a.m. ET, a $70 billion 5-year note auction at 1 p.m., and Dell and Workday after the close.

blocks.head: Stocks cool after the biggest rally in a year and a half
blocks.what: The S&P 500 jumped 4.73% on Monday to 7,237.17, its second-largest point gain ever, and the Nasdaq Composite rose 6.51% to 24,089.56, its best day since April 9, 2025. The Dow added 1,448 points, or 3.01%, to 49,595.31. The rally snapped a seven-session losing streak for the S&P 500 and followed the Nasdaq's 10% drop last week. This morning, futures are giving back part of those gains: S&P 500 futures were down roughly 0.7% to 1% depending on the time of the quote, Dow futures about 0.4% to 0.5%, and CNBC reported Nasdaq 100 futures down as much as about 2%.
blocks.why: A pullback after a one-day move this large is common, and the question for today is whether buyers return to chip and AI stocks or keep taking profits. The VIX volatility index fell to about 27 from near 36, but that is still well above calm-market levels, so large swings in either direction remain likely.
blocks.watch: Whether the Nasdaq holds above Monday's open; a deeper slide would suggest Monday was mostly short covering.

blocks.head: Nvidia slips after its best day since 2003
blocks.what: Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO and board chair on Monday, 11 days after he resigned following his acknowledgment of an affair with a former Megaspeed executive. President Trump said he and his administration assured the board that Huang posed no national security risk, and the WSJ and NYT reported that Vice President Vance helped persuade the board. The shares rose 31.48% to $165.05, adding close to $1 trillion in market value, and set a record for single-stock options volume, per CNBC. Pre-market, the stock is down about 3% to 5%.
blocks.why: Nvidia is the largest weight in the S&P 500 and the bellwether for AI spending, so its direction carries the Nasdaq, chipmakers and AI-linked utilities and industrials. Lawmakers from both parties have criticized the reinstatement and several investigations of the company and Huang remain open, which leaves headline risk in place.
blocks.watch: TechCrunch and others report Huang is scheduled to testify before a Senate committee next week; Senate Banking had requested a December 3 appearance.

blocks.head: Sanofi agrees to buy Insmed for about $41 billion
blocks.what: Sanofi will pay $175 a share in cash for Insmed, a total equity value of about $41 billion, according to Sanofi's announcement. That is about 46% above Insmed's price on November 18, before reports of talks. The deal, approved by both boards, gives Sanofi the lung-disease drugs Brinsupri and Arikayce and is expected to close in the first half of 2027, funded by debt and cash. CNBC described it as the drug industry's biggest deal in three years.
blocks.why: Insmed is up about 14% pre-market and Sanofi rose more than 4% in Europe, per Reuters. The deal adds to a busy stretch of large-scale M&A, after CrowdStrike's $43.9 billion Zscaler deal on Monday, and could lift other mid-size biotech stocks seen as possible targets.
blocks.watch: Antitrust review and whether any rival bidder emerges; Insmed would owe a $1.125 billion fee to back out for a better offer.

blocks.head: Fed hike expectations hold as Williams talks tougher
blocks.what: New York Fed President John Williams said Monday that policy needs to bring inflation back to 2% in a timely way and that higher rates are likely needed over time, per CNBC. He said he would not rule out moving at consecutive meetings if needed, though he did not commit on the December decision. Fed funds futures price about a 95% to 96% chance of a quarter-point hike at the December 8-9 meeting, according to CME FedWatch data cited in several reports.
blocks.why: A hike is largely priced, so markets are now focused on how many more follow. Yahoo Finance reported Monday's rebound revived bets on at least two more increases, which keeps pressure on high-valuation growth stocks and short-term Treasury yields.
blocks.watch: Wednesday's October PCE inflation report, the Fed's preferred gauge.

blocks.head: Hormuz mine claims barely move oil
blocks.what: Iran's Revolutionary Guard said three tankers hit mines and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz on Monday despite US escorts, a claim not independently verified. The US Treasury widened sanctions on more than two dozen Iranian exchange houses and front companies, and the WSJ reported US officials are examining whether Iran was behind cyberattacks on as many as 50 ships. Even so, Brent crude is near $89.40 a barrel, close to its lowest level since late August, per Reuters and others.
blocks.why: Ample supply, including strategic reserve releases cited by a UBS analyst, is outweighing the security risk for now. That keeps pressure on energy stocks, which fell Monday, and helps ease inflation worries ahead of the Fed meeting.
blocks.watch: Any confirmed damage to shipping traffic through Hormuz, which could reverse the calm quickly.

blocks.head: Washington blacklists Megaspeed
blocks.what: The Commerce Department added Megaspeed, the Singapore-based firm at the center of the Nvidia controversy, and six other companies to its entity list over concerns about diversion of advanced computing products, according to CNBC, The Hill and the BBC. US companies now need a special license to do business with them.
blocks.why: The move adds to the debate over chip exports to China, a risk for Nvidia and other chipmakers' sales in Asia. It also signals the administration is pairing its support for Huang with tougher enforcement on the companies involved.

blocks.text: Asia

Asian chip stocks staged a catch-up rally after Wall Street's surge. Taiwan's Taiex climbed about 9%, led by gains near 10% in TSMC and MediaTek, per AP. South Korea's Kospi jumped about 7% to back above 5,000, as Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix rose more than 8% at their highs. Japan's Nikkei 225, back from Monday's holiday, gained about 4% to near 58,645, with chip-equipment makers Advantest up 12.5% and Tokyo Electron up 7.7%. Hong Kong was the exception: the Hang Seng fell nearly 1% to its lowest level in more than a year, while Shanghai edged up about 0.3%.
Europe

European stocks are roughly flat after Monday's strongest session in about six months, when the Stoxx 600 rose about 1.9% and Germany's DAX about 2.2%. Reuters reported the Stoxx 600 slipping about 0.2% in morning trade as the tech rally faded. Chip stocks lost ground: Aixtron fell almost 9% after UBS downgraded it to sell, and Infineon and STMicroelectronics eased. Sanofi was among the top gainers on the Insmed deal. London's FTSE 100 is slightly lower.
Currencies

The dollar is a little weaker, with the dollar index down about 0.2% near 104.1. The euro is up about 0.3% near $1.094 and the pound up about 0.3% near $1.307. The yen remains weak as safe-haven demand fades: the dollar is near 159.3 yen, close to the 160 level that traders watch for possible Japanese intervention after Tokyo spent about ¥15.4 trillion supporting the yen in July and August. The dollar is flat against China's yuan near 6.66.

US futures point to a lower open, with tech leading the decline. As of the latest readings before 8 a.m. ET, S&P 500 futures were down about 0.7% to 1% and Dow futures about 0.4% to 0.5%, while Nasdaq 100 futures were down more, between about 1% and 2% depending on the source and time. That would leave the S&P 500 well above Friday's close of 6,910 even after the dip, since Monday's gain was more than 4.5%.

The pattern this morning is a partial reversal of Monday: Nvidia and other chipmakers are lower, while retail stocks with strong earnings, such as Dollar Tree, and deal targets like Insmed are higher. Small caps, which rose about 3.4% on Monday, are likely to track the broader market. Holiday-thinned trading this week can make moves larger than usual.

Treasury yields are slightly lower. The 2-year yield is near 4.64%, down about 3 basis points, the 10-year near 4.90%, down about 2 basis points, and the 30-year near 5.28%, down about 2 basis points. CNBC tied the move to digesting Williams's remarks ahead of today's 5-year note auction. The curve remains modestly upward sloping: the 10-year pays about 26 basis points more than the 2-year, and the 30-year about 64 basis points more. Deutsche Bank, in a forecast reported by the WSJ, expects the 10-year to end 2027 near 5.05%.

Markets treat a December hike as close to certain. CME FedWatch data cited by several outlets show roughly a 95% to 96% chance of a quarter-point increase at the December 8-9 meeting, with a small chance of a half point. Governor Christopher Waller has floated a larger move, while Williams said he would not exclude hiking at back-to-back meetings. Wednesday's PCE inflation data and the Beige Book are the last major inputs before the Fed's quiet period begins Saturday.
Fed and Treasury events today

items: No Fed speeches are confirmed on today's schedule; reports conflicted on whether Williams appears again.
1 p.m. ET: Treasury sells $70 billion of 5-year notes; the prior sale yielded 4.845%. Weak demand could push yields higher.
Also today: a $28 billion 2-year floating-rate note auction.

blocks.text: Sectors (Monday's session)

Technology led Monday by a wide margin, with the sector fund up about 9% as chipmakers rebounded behind Nvidia. Consumer discretionary and industrials each gained close to 4%, communication services about 3.6% and materials about 3.2%, all groups tied to AI spending or the big tech stocks. Defensive sectors lagged: health care, utilities and real estate rose about 1% to 1.5%, consumer staples were flat and energy was the only sector to fall, down about 1% as oil slid. Advancers beat decliners in the S&P 500 by about 5 to 1. Today's futures suggest a partial reversal, with tech under pressure.
Pre-market movers

items: Nvidia: down about 3% to 5% after Monday's 31.5% jump.
Insmed: up about 14% on Sanofi's $175-a-share cash offer.
Dollar Tree: up roughly 10% after adjusted earnings of $1.16 a share beat the roughly $0.91 to $0.92 expected; it raised its full-year profit outlook to $8.05 to $8.25 a share.

Analog Devices: down about 7% after its first-quarter revenue forecast of $4.25 billion to $4.55 billion implied little growth from the fourth quarter, despite a beat with adjusted EPS of $4.06 on $4.37 billion in revenue.
Hewlett Packard Enterprise: lower again after falling Monday despite raising its forecast on AI demand.
Dell: rose about 20% Monday on the Huang news ahead of tonight's report.

blocks.text: Oil

Crude is little changed, with Brent near $89.40 a barrel and WTI near $80.10. Brent is near its lowest level since late August and well below October's high near $105. Supply is the main driver: strategic reserve releases and forecasts of a surplus are offsetting Iran's claim that three tankers hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz. Some analysts, including Eurasia Group, warn that a sustained increase in attacks could change that balance.
Gold

Gold is down about 0.7% near $3,624 an ounce, giving back part of Monday's bounce. Expectations of more Fed hikes make a metal that pays no interest less attractive, and the return of risk appetite has cut demand for havens. Gold remains far below its January record above $5,500.
Crypto

Bitcoin is down about 2.4% near $59,650 and Ether down about 2.5% near $1,680, both reversing part of Monday's rebound. Bitcoin hit a roughly two-year low near $55,100 on Saturday. Crypto has tracked tech stocks closely during the selloff, and continued outflows from spot bitcoin ETFs have been cited as a drag.
A moderate day for data; the bond auction and after-hours earnings may matter more than the numbers:

items: 10 a.m. ET: Conference Board consumer confidence for November, forecast at 92.4 versus 91.7 last month. A weaker reading would fit the picture of cautious shoppers heading into Black Friday.
9 a.m. ET: S&P/Case-Shiller home prices, expected up 2.7% from a year earlier, unchanged from the prior month.
10 a.m. ET: Richmond Fed manufacturing index, forecast at -2.
After the close: Dell, Workday, Autodesk and HP report.

blocks.text: A busy day for retail and tech. Several before-the-open reports were still being digested as this was written; figures below are only those confirmed in company releases or at least two outlets.

rows: AI server orders and backlog, which stood at about $95 billion, and gross margins as memory costs rise. Dell guided to about $49 billion in revenue and $6.50 a share; consensus is about $6.62. Options imply a move of roughly 13%.

Subscription growth versus its 12% guide and signs AI is helping or hurting business software demand. Analysts expect about $2.74 a share on $2.69 billion in revenue; the stock is down about 25% from its 2026 high.
Beat on earnings and revenue, but a cautious first-quarter outlook has the stock lower; a read on industrial and auto chip demand.
Fiscal second-quarter results, due at 6:45 a.m. ET; watch organic growth versus its full-year target of 6.75% to 7.25%.
Earnings beat and raised full-year outlook; a gauge of how lower-income shoppers are holding up.
Holiday-quarter outlooks and comments on consumer demand heading into Black Friday.

blocks.text: This is a holiday-shortened week: US markets are closed Thursday for Thanksgiving and close early, at 1 p.m. ET, on Friday. Wednesday is the main event, with a cluster of 8:30 a.m. ET releases moved up before the holiday: the second estimate of third-quarter GDP, forecast at 3.5% annualized; October PCE inflation, with core prices expected up 0.3% for the month; personal income and spending, each forecast up 0.4%; durable goods orders; and weekly jobless claims, expected near 201,000. New home sales follow at 10 a.m. and the Fed's Beige Book at 2 p.m. A hot PCE reading would firm up bets on hikes beyond December. Black Friday sales will offer an early read on holiday spending, and Huang's planned Senate testimony next week keeps Nvidia in focus.

bottom_line: After Monday's surge, the tone is a modest pullback led by the same chip stocks that rallied most, while bonds are steady and Fed hike expectations are unchanged. Tonight's Dell and Workday results and Wednesday's PCE data are the next tests of whether the rebound holds.
